Hands of vast teams of engineers now learn complex tasks. Robot hands are evolving, with four autonomous fingers that can handle anything from flesh and blood to the stuff of fantasy. Inside the top artificial intelligence labs, researchers are getting closer to creating hands that are the real thing. Inside a San Francisco artificial intelligence lab founded by Elon Musk and several big Silicon Valley names, they find a hand that looks a lot like the mechanical hands from the latest Star Wars film. The mechanical digits bend like a human hand, giving the ability to ask for an alphabet block, show particular letters, and say red, orange, or blue. They can show, spin, twist, and flip in ways a human hand can, completing simple tasks. This autonomous machine represents a notable achievement, having learned tasks largely using methods that allow it to learn. Researchers believe they can train these hands to perform far more complex tasks. Remarkably, this hand represents an enormous leap in research over the last few years. Recently, researchers are still struggling to master many tasks, but much has been created. Researchers in a lab inside the University of California, Berkeley, have developed a system that represents the limits of technology just years ago. Equipped with two machines, it can pick items like a pair and sort them, making it much easier to control than a five-fingered hand. Building software needed to operate it is nearly as difficult as dealing with objects that are slightly unfamiliar. For example, it knows a restaurant-style bottle by its basic shape, but if the machine is confronted with something different, like a plastic bottle, it really wants the robot to pick anything, even stuff it has never seen. Researchers built this system over the last few years, which still uses simple hardware to pick and sort random items like a pair of plastic cups. The system benefits from dramatic advances in machine learning. Berkeley researchers modeled objects, identifying the best way to pick one using a network system that analyzes data to learn how to recognize the best way to pick an item. In the past, researchers programmed robots to perform tasks, but now they learn tasks they are confronted with. For instance, the plastic system recognizes how to pick the faces of a bottle or cup from a bin full of random stuff. This perfect system learns and is improving at a far faster rate than machines in the past. The bed maker robot can make perfect hospital corners, representing notable progress. Berkeley researchers pulled this system together in just two weeks using the latest machine learning techniques. Long ago, this would have taken months or years. Now, the system can learn to make a bed in a fraction of the time, just by analyzing data. In this case, the system's movements lead to making a bed across the Berkeley campus lab. They call another system that applies learning methods to push objects and predict how to move toys across a desk. Much of the system learns behavior by analyzing vast collections of video images showing how objects get pushed and how to deal with unexpected movements. When it comes to kind tasks in the future, simple tasks are what machines can handle, but under certain conditions, they may fail. Much of the machine learning methods drive these systems, pointing to continued progress in the years to come. Like researchers at the University of Washington, they are training hands with digits, which are far more difficult to train. The cup hand moves in many different ways, and Washington researchers train the hand digitally in a real-world training process. Researchers are training the hand in much the same way the system learns to spin an alphabet block. Years of trial and error in digital running across thousands of computer chips allow it to learn in two days. It learns tasks through repeated trial and error and learns how to apply knowledge in the real world. Many researchers have questioned whether this kind of training can transfer to the physical realm, but researchers at Berkeley labs have shown that introducing a certain amount of training can change the friction of the hand on a block or even change gravity. Learning to deal with the world with the hand is a challenge, but they are dealing with a real one.

Inflation is a frequently asked question; inflation represents the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning that a dollar today is worth less than a dollar tomorrow. It is typically expressed as an annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, but inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in little economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. 

Inflation can be bad, but it depends on the circumstances; fast price increases can spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation can also affect the stock market, as rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets. Historically, tangible assets like houses have held their value better during inflation booms.

Madrid: NATO leaders formally invite Finland and Sweden to join the alliance on Wednesday after Turkey lifted its veto on membership, the Secretary General said Tuesday evening, clearing the way for one significant alliance in decades. This historic deal follows a memorandum between the two countries that underscored the war in Ukraine and President Vladimir Putin's Russian efforts to weaken NATO, pushing Sweden and Finland to remain neutral for decades. Arms talks over the weeks culminated in a meeting in Madrid where President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey agreed to lift the block on Sweden's membership in return for actions promised against terrorism and terrorist organizations by NATO allies. Finland and Sweden commit to fully supporting Turkey against threats to national security, the Secretary General said, providing details that the agreement includes domestic legislation cracking down on activities entering the agreement. Turkey's extradition request was added, referring to a party that seeks an independent Kurdish state in territory partly within its borders. Erdogan is blocking NATO bids amid concerns over longtime support for targets that killed civilians in Turkey, which is designated by the United States and the European Union as a terrorist organization. Look, the process of getting a visa to visit the United States is a long, extensive process for much of the world. Visiting the United States means submitting an application, and the process can take months, or even years, and often ends in denial. Even allies like India face challenges. Many countries are singled out by the revised travel ban. The typical process involves submitting a visa application online, paying the application fee at a designated bank, signing up for an interview, and gathering documents to show a stable life. Likely recommended documents include a letter of introduction from an employer, an invitation letter, a passport, bank statements, and anything else that proves the intent to return home after the interview. 

Countries take four months to get an interview appointment date, where you meet a foreign service officer. The officer may deny your request sometimes without even looking at the documents. They also refer the case for a deeper review, and information is checked against American foreign databases. Officers from various agencies also conduct interviews and research background checks. Everything is checked before a visa is issued. At the airport, American customs officers conduct an additional round of behind-the-scenes screening upon arrival and question travelers. 

Applications are denied at the highest refusal rates in the fiscal year for Somalia, Cuba, Syria, Afghanistan, and El Salvador. The refusal rates for these countries in the fiscal year from October to September are noted by the State Department's Bureau of Consular Affairs. The rates for visas for tourist and business visitors vary by country, and applicants are typically told they are denied if the denial rate is high. The highest rates are found in African and Middle Eastern countries, including Syria, Somalia, and Cuba, which also have high denial rates for entering without a visa. 

Visitors from countries that are members of the visa program must still provide personal information to the American government before boarding a plane to the United States. Many citizens from Canada also visit the United States without a visa. Members of the visa program in Europe include Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom. In Asia, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Singapore, South Korea, and Taiwan are included. South American travelers from countries in the visa program can visit the United States for days without a visa, which is a shorter process and requires paying a smaller fee for a visa. 

Travelers can apply for travel authorization by submitting personal information, including employment, diseases, and criminal history. Upon arriving, Customs and Border Protection officers make the final decision regarding entry into the United States. The eligibility for certain visitors changed last year after the Paris attacks, as people who traveled to Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, or Yemen since then became ineligible.

Inflation FAQ card: Inflation is the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning the dollar today is worth less than it was yesterday. Typically, it is expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. 

The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, but inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Whether inflation is bad depends on the circumstances; fast price increases can spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. 

Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation can also affect the stock market; rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms. Tangible assets like houses have held their value better. 

Fed leadership has sharply reduced unemployment while maintaining control of inflation, coming close to achieving its congressional mandate. Many Americans buy a gun in less than an hour, while in other countries the process can take weeks or months. To buy a gun in the United States, one must pass an instant background check that considers criminal convictions, domestic violence, and immigration status. In many states, there are additional buying restrictions, including waiting periods and expanded background checks. Roughly a third of American gun owners buy guns without a background check, as federal law requires buying directly from a private seller. In Japan, to take a firearm class, one must pass a written exam held three times a year, get a note saying they are mentally fit, have no history of drug abuse, apply for a permit, take firing training, and then wait a month to describe to the police why they need a gun. They must pass a review of their criminal history, gun possession record, employment, involvement with organized crime groups, personal debt, and relationships with friends, family, and neighbors. To apply for a permit, one must take a one-day training class, pass a firing test, and obtain a certificate from a gun dealer describing the gun they want. If they want a gun for hunting, they must apply for a hunting license and buy a safe for ammunition that meets safety regulations to allow police to check gun storage. They must also pass an additional background review to buy a gun. In countries that require buyers to accurately hit a target, they must demonstrate safe handling procedures. In New Zealand, one must pass a background check that considers criminal, medical, and mental health records, as well as domestic violence records, and provide character references. Authorities will interview the person and their partner, and then they must pass a home security inspection that checks for proper firearm storage. They must take a gun safety course and wait for approval of their firearms license, which can take weeks or months. After the shooting of two mosques in New Zealand, a law was passed banning certain weapons, making gun regulations in New Zealand far more restrictive than in the United States. Buying a gun requires a special permit, unlike in countries like New Zealand that require guns to be registered. In South Africa, one must join a hunting or shooting club and document the need for self-defense, complete firearm safety training, and pass a written test and practical assessment. They must provide two references from employers, friends, or community leaders to get a pass for a review of their criminal behavior history, including domestic violence and drug abuse cases, and undergo interviews with family and neighbors. To buy a gun that is safe and meets safety regulations, one must wait several months for federal review of their application. In Mexico, authorities require a letter from local authorities confirming any criminal record, and buyers must submit a letter showing their employment status to pay and pass a background check that considers their criminal history and employment. Current gun ownership is also a factor when traveling to Mexico City, where stores authorized to sell guns are located. In Mexico, Russia, and South Africa, there are thriving black markets for guns, while one store in Mexico sells guns legally compared to retail stores in the United States. In Australia, one must join and regularly attend a hunting or shooting club, document completion of a course in firearm safety and operation, pass a written test and practical assessment, and arrange for firearm storage that meets safety regulations. They must also pass a review that considers their criminal history and any domestic violence orders or arrest history, and authorities will interview family and community members. To apply for a permit to acquire a specific type of weapon, one must wait at least 28 days to buy that specific type of gun after receiving a permit. In response to a mass shooting, Australia officially made gun ownership a privilege, requiring gun owners to provide a valid reason for owning a weapon, such as farming, hunting, or membership in gun clubs. In Austria, one must get a handgun or rifle by proving they are in serious physical danger, passing a review of their criminal history, filling out a mental health survey, completing a psychological and physical test, and completing a course on safe gun handling and storage. They must install safe gun storage, and if they buy a gun, they must wait three days before coming back to pick it up. Austria requires different steps to get a hunting rifle, including passing a written exam and shooting test. These periods are intended to reduce the likelihood of violence. In Canada, to buy a handgun, one must prove they practice at an approved shooting club or range, show their gun, complete a safety course, and pass a written and practical test. They must ask for two references when applying for a permit, and wait 28 days for processing to begin. They must also pass a background check that considers their criminal record, mental health, addiction, and domestic violence history. After buying a gun, they must register it with the police when taking it home. In addition, two character references are required, and Canadians must list the names of partners they have lived with in the last two years and sign the application to notify the police of the gun they bought. In India, one must join a shooting club, show that there is a property threat, attend a practical training course in firearm handling and shooting, and obtain a certificate from a physical and mental health doctor. They must have a safe place to keep firearms and pass a review that considers their last three years of tax returns, criminal history, mental health history, and domestic violence, which includes interviews with family and neighbors. The exact steps in India can vary depending on local officials and how they choose to enforce the law. Indian authorities may use guns during elections to ensure voting is peaceful, and guns must be returned to owners within one week after results are announced. In Germany, one must join a shooting club to obtain a hunting license, demonstrate that their life is threatened, and demonstrate specialized knowledge of firearms, which involves a written exam and practical demonstration of safe handling. They must submit a certificate of mental fitness from a public health officer or doctor, arrange for proper firearm storage, and pass a background check that considers their criminal history and mental health. To apply for a permit to purchase a specific gun, one must include an additional short background review. In Germany, citizens keep firearms in their homes and agree to let police conduct unannounced home inspections to check that they are kept safely. In Britain, one must join a shooting club and document their hunting arrangements, ask for a character reference, and arrange for proper firearm storage. A background check includes a police interview, and home storage arrangements are checked before one can buy a gun. In Brazil, one must write a statement explaining the need for a gun for self-defense, complete a course in firearm handling, and demonstrate a strike from feet away with at least 70 percent accuracy. They must obtain a statement from a psychologist certifying they are mentally fit to fire a weapon, and obtain a certificate confirming no criminal investigation. To buy a gun, one must register it with the federal police and fill out an online form to order transport of the gun back to the dealer to pick it up. Brazil requires authorization every time one transports a gun, including the first time taking it home. In Russia, one must get a hunting license, explain the need for a gun for self-defense, pass a test on relevant laws and handling, and first aid skills, and get a note saying they have a history of mental illness or drug abuse. They must attend a firearm safety handling class and pass an exam to apply for a license and pass a background check to buy a gun. Many Russian gun buyers skip the process and obtain illegal guns. In Russia, it is estimated that legal guns are a factor. In Israel, one must join a shooting club and prove they live or work in a dangerous area to obtain authorized gun ownership, including in certain settlements. They must get a note saying they have a history of mental illness or drug abuse and install a gun safe. They must release their criminal and mental health history to the authorities to buy a gun. There is a limited supply of bullets, and they usually must demonstrate the use of a gun similar to a gun firing range before taking it home. Many countries, including Israel, also allow people in certain jobs to easily obtain guns, including for security or research. In China, one must establish a specific reason to possess a firearm for hunting or sports shooting, arrange to store the gun at a gun range or remote hunting ground area, and demonstrate knowledge of safe gun use and storage. They must pass a background check that considers mental illness and criminal records, including domestic violence. To buy a gun in China, civilians are prohibited from keeping guns in their homes, and guns must be kept at authorized locations. In Yemen, the gun market is where one can find a seller online to buy a gun. Yemen has the second highest gun ownership rate in the world, and Yemeni law states that buyers must obtain guns from licensed dealers and register with the authorities. The law is largely unregulated.

The full transcript of the statement on the Russia investigation is as follows: Good morning, everyone. Thank you. Two years ago, the Acting Attorney General asked me to serve as Special Counsel, which created a special office. The appointment order directed the office to investigate Russian interference in the presidential election, which included investigating links and coordination between the Russian government and individuals associated with the Trump campaign. I have now spoken publicly about the investigation, and I am speaking today because the investigation is complete. The Attorney General has made the report of the investigation largely public, formally closing the special office and resigning from the Department of Justice to return to private life. I will make remarks on the results of our work, but beyond my remarks, it is important that the written work speaks for itself. Let me begin. 

The appointment order begins with the interference in the presidential election, which was alleged in a grand jury indictment against Russian intelligence officers, part of the Russian military, who launched a concerted attack on our political system. The indictment describes how they used sophisticated cyber techniques to hack into computers and networks, including those used by the Clinton campaign, and how private information was released. The information was released through fake online identities and the organization WikiLeaks, and these releases were designed to be timed to interfere with the election and damage a presidential candidate. 

The grand jury issued a separate indictment against a private Russian entity that engaged in a social media operation where Russian citizens posed as Americans in order to influence the election. The indictments contain allegations of guilt, but the innocence of each specific defendant is presumed until proven guilty. The activities described in the report outline the efforts to interfere with our political system, which needed to be investigated. It is understood that among the reasons the Department of Justice established this office, there was also a reason to investigate efforts to obstruct the investigation into these matters. 

It is critically important to obtain full and accurate information from every person questioned in the subject of the investigation. The investigation lies at the core of our effort to find the truth and hold those accountable. Let me say a word about the report. The report has two parts, addressing two main issues that we were asked to investigate. The first volume of the report details the numerous efforts by Russia to influence the election. This volume includes a discussion of the Trump campaign's response to this activity and concludes that there is insufficient evidence to charge a broader conspiracy. The second volume of the report describes the results and analysis of obstruction of justice in the investigation involving the President. 

The order appointing the Special Counsel authorized us to investigate actions that may obstruct the investigation. The investigation was kept from the office of the Acting Attorney General to ensure progress. The work set forth in the report reflects the investigation's confidence that the President clearly committed a crime. However, we make no determination on whether the President committed a crime. The introduction of the volume of the report explains our decision and explains longstanding Department policy that a President cannot be charged with a federal crime while in office. 

Even if we could charge a sitting President, the decision to keep the charge sealed and hidden from public view is prohibited by the special office's part of Department of Justice regulation. We are bound by Department policy regarding charging a President with a crime. Therefore, the option to consider a written opinion explaining this policy makes several important points. The first opinion explicitly permits the investigation of a sitting President, which is important to preserve evidence while memories are fresh and documents are available. Among other things, this evidence could be used to charge the President. 

The second opinion states that the Constitution requires a process in the criminal justice system to formally accuse a sitting President of wrongdoing. Beyond the Department policy, we are guided by principles of fairness, which could potentially be unfair if we were to accuse someone of a crime without a court resolution. The actual charge is governed by Department policy principles. We concluded that we could not reach a determination one way or the other on whether the President committed a crime. 

My final position is to comment on the conclusions of the President's conduct. An independent criminal investigation was conducted, and the results were reported to the Attorney General as required by Department regulations. The Attorney General concluded that it was appropriate to provide a report to Congress and the American people. At one point in time, certain portions of the report were requested to be released, and the Attorney General preferred to make the entire report public. I appreciate that the Attorney General made the report largely public. 

There is certainly a question regarding the Attorney General's good faith decision, and now I hope and expect that when I speak in this manner, I will be told whether I can testify or speak on this matter. The discussion of my appearance before Congress and testimony goes beyond the report, which contains findings, analysis, and reasons for the decisions made. I chose my words carefully, and the work speaks for itself. The report and testimony provide information beyond what is already public. My appearance before Congress, in addition to access to the underlying work product, is decided by the process involved in the office. Beyond what I said today, I believe it is appropriate to speak about the investigation and comment on the actions of the Justice Department. For this reason, I am taking questions today. 

Now, I will step away. I want to thank the attorneys, FBI agents, analysts, and professional staff who helped conduct the investigation in a fair and independent manner. These individuals spent nearly two years in the special office with the highest integrity, and the close central allegation of the indictments regarding multiple systematic efforts to interfere with the election deserves the attention of every American. Thank you. Thank you for today.

Inflation FAQ card: Inflation is the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning a dollar today typically buys less than it did a year ago. Inflation is usually expressed as an annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, but inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Whether inflation is bad depends on the circumstances; fast price increases can spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. 

Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market; rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms. Tangible assets like houses have held their value better.

Early employees who joined the company several years ago received stock options that allowed them to buy shares at a low price as part of their compensation packages. Inflation FAQ: Inflation is the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning a dollar today is worth less than a dollar tomorrow. It is typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, including food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, and inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. 

Inflation is bad and depends on circumstances; fast price increases spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market; rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms. Tangible assets like houses have held their value better.

Inflation FAQ card: Inflation is the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning a dollar today is worth far less than tomorrow. It is typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, but inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in little economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Whether inflation is bad depends on the circumstances; fast price increases can spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation can also affect the stock market; rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better. Antitrust fines were third imposed on Google by the European Union since its regulatory role as an aggressive tech watchdog. Google was fined a billion for unfair advertising rules last year, and it was fined a record billion for using its ownership of the Android mobile operating system to unfairly undercut rivals in the mobile phone market. This decision also forced the company to change apps on smartphones. The company was fined a billion euros for unfairly favoring shopping services over rivals in two previous rulings, which had a big impact on its financial health and forced the tech giant to adjust its business practices. The Android ruling last year marked the first time Google began charging makers to pre-install Google Maps and other popular applications on Android devices. The European Union may be attempting to head off additional inquiries, as Google announced a number of changes to its services across Europe on Wednesday. Rivals complained that they continued to be disadvantaged by Google's business practices. For the first time, the company said it would ask Android phone users in Europe if they want to switch to a web search engine not owned by Google, allowing competition and enabling customers to shop. Google also stated that local search in Europe would help a person searching for a restaurant to find options outside of its own services. The review practices of Google and others are under scrutiny as the European Union adopted tough new privacy rules, and many countries outside Europe are now viewing regulators with increased scrutiny. The decision on Wednesday regarding Google was one of the final major antitrust rulings in a five-year term during which the crackdown on Silicon Valley was led by a competition commissioner who has become a minor celebrity in the world of European politics.

Mayor Bill de Blasio of New York City laid out a series of long-awaited safety protocols for schools on Thursday, seeking to reassure parents concerned that the Delta variant of the coronavirus could upend the school year. The announcement follows weeks of rising alarm from parents and educators about the plan to reopen schools at full capacity without a remote learning option. The first day of school for roughly a million students is on September 13, and a child inside a classroom this year and a half is supposed to happen. "Let it not happen anymore," de Blasio said at a news conference. As part of the new protocols, the city will test a random sample of 10 percent of unvaccinated people in schools every week. The group will include students, and later in the fall, adults will be required to be fully vaccinated, the mayor said. This means children in elementary school will be subjected to testing pending parent consent, while unvaccinated middle and high school students will be tested. Children older than 12 are eligible to get vaccinated since mid-May, but it remains unclear when younger children will become eligible. The testing program is of modest scope compared to last year, with roughly 30 percent fewer children in schools as many families chose remote learning last school year. The city initially tested 20 percent of people in schools, which increased to 40 percent in spring after the mayor relaxed the rules. The mayor defended the plan on Thursday, saying the city needs much testing as many students are vaccinated. He said the city will increase testing in schools and neighborhoods as needed. De Blasio is also aiming to avoid frequent classroom closures, which proved disruptive to children and educators last school year. Last year, when someone in a classroom tested positive, unvaccinated close contacts had to quarantine for 10 days. It is unclear what is considered a close contact, as the system is conservative. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that health officials strike a balance between safety and disruption. The mayor also hopes to avoid the bitter fights over masks and vaccinations in schools that have roiled many areas, as districts across the country have adopted a range of approaches in response to the threat of Delta. Plans have been heavily shaped by the politics of parents, as districts controlled by Republican mayors and governors pushed back against restrictions. Middle and high school students in New York City who are unvaccinated will be considered close contacts of an infected person but can leave quarantine early if they receive a negative test result after five days. Quarantine buildings will close for 10 days if evidence of widespread transmission is determined by disease detectives. Elementary school students learning from home during quarantine will receive live online instruction, while teachers quarantined will provide older students with work assignments from home. The city still has details to work out with unions about teaching remote classes. The city is planning to expand an existing program that allows vulnerable children to get 15 hours of in-person home instruction per week, while online learning will be available for students who qualify for the program this year compared to previous years. The city expects several thousand students to participate. Students and staff will be required to wear masks in the classroom, and there will be two air purifiers instructed to keep three feet of distance between students wherever possible. City officials said distancing is possible in the vast majority of classrooms. Recent federal guidance called for universal masking in schools regardless of vaccination status, with a focus on returning to in-person learning this fall. City schools saw extremely low virus transmission last year, with a test positivity rate at the end of the school year in June.

Track COVID area to get the latest state and county data on cases, deaths, hospitalizations, tests, and vaccinations. The coronavirus latest map shows case count data sources from state and local health agencies, including cases, deaths, and the Department of Health and Human Services. Test positivity, hospitalizations, and ICU patients are tracked with a seven-day average based on recent seven days of data figures. COVID patients in hospitals show the recent number of patients hospitalized with COVID in the intensive care unit. Day spikes occur due to inconsistent reporting from hospitals, and hospitalization numbers early in the pandemic were affected by incomplete reporting from hospitals. The federal government tracks test positivity based on viral tests from tested laboratories, while state health departments report to the federal government. States, including Washington and Puerto Rico, report hospitalizations and test positivity based on assigned dates from the Department of Health and Human Services, which is subject to historical revisions. Cases and deaths data are assigned dates based on figures publicly reported, including case and death seven-day averages. Days within the range of data reported during the period are extended to older days, with at least seven days of data included. Data from days following non-reporting days are averaged, and non-reporting days are included in rolling averages representing multiple days' worth of data. This means that in instances of timed reporting, the seven-day average is calculated based on the average of seven days, while certain days' total case and death reports are excluded from the average. A portion of cases and deaths data is removed from the average calculation to create a national case and death count average, which is the sum of the average number of cases and deaths across states and territories. The day average matches the average calculated for case and death totals in order to account for timed case and death reports at the state level.

Knowing the amount of virus carried in the body can help doctors predict the course of illness in infected coronavirus patients. As COVID patients flood hospitals nationwide, doctors are facing an impossible question: which patients are likely to quickly fight the virus and recover? This turns out to help distinguish the two groups. Although it is not yet widely employed, dozens of research papers published in the past months have found that people whose bodies carry a lot of coronavirus often become seriously ill and are likely to die, compared to those who carry much less virus and are likely to emerge relatively unscathed. The results suggest that knowing the so-called viral load, or the amount of virus in the body, can help doctors predict the course of illness and the need for oxygen. Just a day ago, for example, a patient needed to be monitored closely, said Daniel, an infectious disease physician at Columbia University in New York. Tracking viral load can actually help assess risk, he said. The idea is new, but managing viral load has long formed the basis of care for people with HIV, for example, in terms of transmission of the virus.

The Apple Watch points to the future, yet almost eight months in, the Apple Watch feels like the future of anything else. Inflation is a FAQ card. Inflation means the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning a dollar today is worth less than a dollar tomorrow. It is typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, but inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in little economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Whether inflation is bad depends on the circumstances; fast price increases spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. 

Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation can also affect the stock market; rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms. Tangible assets like houses have held their value better.

Mrs. Thatcher set the country on an economic path and held the top office longer than any British politician in the century. Margaret Thatcher set Britain on a new course as inflation rose, reversed, and raised interest rates in a sudden effort to control the money flow, which threw Britain into recession. In October, she resigned, and many devoted supporters admitted they bore much blame, laying it at her door for the effort to make local authorities accountable for the way they spent tax money. Mrs. Thatcher pushed a measure that replaced property taxes with a community tax intended to make everyone, not just property owners, pay for local government services; in practice, this measure was unfair and deeply unpopular. In March, protests and riots erupted within the party, and there was a growing feeling that the Iron Lady had become a liability. By fall, in November, tensions among the party exploded when the Deputy Prime Minister, the last original member of the Thatcher cabinet known for his loyalty, though he disagreed with her prime policy toward Europe, saw the differences come to a boil at a cabinet meeting. Incredibly, Kenneth Baker and another minister recalled that the last had resigned the next day. Michael, a former defense minister, favored greater links with Europe and announced a challenge to Mrs. Thatcher for the party leadership. In November, the Prime Minister was attending a summit meeting in Paris when a vote was taken; Mrs. Thatcher, whose approval ratings in the polls were falling, faced a bleak outcome. Though she beat the votes, the party rules required a majority strong enough to keep her place, and the race was now wide open. It took an unexpected turn when Mrs. Thatcher, awaiting the results of the party ballot with family and friends at Downing Street, learned she had lost. The soft-spoken Chancellor, John Major, said someone had done an awful turn, and she replied that politics was like that. Though vowing to fight in the second ballot, she was persuaded to withdraw. Speaking to the Queen and calling world leaders, she made her final speech in the House of Commons and resigned in November, leaving Downing Street in tears and feeling betrayed. After leaving office, Mrs. Thatcher traveled widely, drew huge crowds on the circuit, and sat for the House. Thatcher wrote a memoir devoted to the Margaret Thatcher Foundation and its values.

Change in companies' value investments can cause major earnings reports due to a little-known accounting change with a big impact. This update will significantly affect the way companies like Alphabet, Intel, and IBM make a lot of small investments, as companies report earnings and also curtail investments made in the first place. Businesses say the costs of complying with the rule are high, but things change with the new rule. Now, when a company buys a stake of less than a percent in another company, it usually accounts for the investment on the balance sheet at the cost price paid at the time. Under the old rules, the value of the investment goes up, but the new rules require writing the value on the income statement and balance sheet. If the value increases over time, the investment is still kept at cost, which leaves investors fully informed; however, if the investment lost value, there is less transparency. If the investment increased in value, investors lost transparency on the upside, which is argued to have gained requiring corporate executives to place a number that is often difficult to value for investments every quarter. This is going to change, as a minority investment in a public company is now valued quarterly, whether the value increased or decreased, leading to potential volatility. It will soon be required to flow into the income statement, possibly causing earnings per share to fluctuate, something even core business corporate executives will have to manage. They have two choices for investments: either spend time on investments or hire an accounting firm or valuation firm, or choose to wait for a market-driven valuation event to mark the value of the investment. The company chooses how to value investments, whether every quarter or based on a market event selected, and this will soon change, adding to corporate concerns.

Biden calls Colin Powell an honor, and images of vaccines are critical in reducing severe disease and death from coronavirus. Still, outcomes are unexpected, health experts say. Credit Patrick Agence France Presse, Getty Images. The death of former Secretary of State Colin Powell on Monday from complications of COVID provided fuel that vaccine opponents immediately seized. The news that Powell was vaccinated stoked doubts about the effectiveness of vaccines. His immune system was likely weakened by multiple cancer treatments, which affect white blood cells and make people susceptible to infections. Age also increases risk, scientists said. Powell received his second dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine in February, said a longtime aide, and he was scheduled for a booster last week but fell ill before receiving it. Although the death of such a high-profile figure is a tragedy, scientists stressed that it does not undermine confidence in COVID vaccines, which drastically reduce the odds of severe disease and death. "They are 95 percent effective," said Paul, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Hospital of Philadelphia. "At this point, getting the vaccine, you want to know the benefits clearly outweigh the risks. We know vaccines are highly effective, even against the contagious Delta variant, which is now responsible for nearly all infections in the United States. People who are fully vaccinated are roughly three times less likely to be hospitalized and ten times less likely to die from COVID, according to a recent study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention." A New York Times analysis of data from states found that fully vaccinated people accounted for 1.3 percent of COVID deaths among 100 million Americans fully vaccinated. According to the CDC, five percent of deaths are among people over 65, and deaths among vaccinated individuals occur, said Peter Dean from the National School of Tropical Medicine at the College of Medicine. Certain groups are at greater risk. Since the beginning of the pandemic, it has been clear that older adults are likely to develop severe COVID and also have less robust immune systems in general, which mount a weaker immune response to vaccines. One recent study, yet to be reviewed by experts, found that residents of Canadian long-term care homes with a median age of 84 produced levels of antibodies that were roughly five times lower than those of vaccinated staff members, whose median age is 45. This puts them at risk of getting infected with COVID and having severe consequences, said Anne, a senior investigator at the Research Institute at Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto and lead author of the study. Powell also underwent treatment for multiple cancer types, which affect white blood cells that make antibodies and thus play a critical role in the immune system. Such disease treatments include those that leave patients vulnerable to infections. "Undergoing treatment for multiple myeloma seemed to be responding," Kathy, who founded a multiple myeloma research foundation, said. She met Powell and spoke at a foundation event. "It is a reminder that patients are at high risk, especially those over 65. Vaccines are also likely less effective in people with multiple myeloma and a normal immune system," said James, the medical scientific director at the Institute for Bone Cancer Research in West Hollywood. A study published in July by colleagues found that just 43 percent of active multiple myeloma patients were adequately receiving the Pfizer or Moderna vaccines. People who received the Pfizer vaccine had lower antibody levels than Moderna recipients on average. Researchers found that older patients also had lower antibody levels. It is unclear what kind of treatment Powell received or whether he was fully vaccinated, even though patients with compromised immune systems usually maintain an immune state and have a good response to treatment, said Eric. Climate change discussions take center stage in Glasgow, and you are likely to hear a lot about climate searching for hidden meaning in the climate search for net zero, sustainability, nature-based solutions, adaptation, and carbon footprint. Electric natural gas governments are committing to net zero, and sustainable products are sold on Instagram. Banks pushing climate change get worse, and it seems like everyone wants to know something about what the words really mean, while we are communicating information. There is a long history of choosing words meant to advance an agenda; two decades ago, a man named Frank famously advised Republicans to say "climate change" instead of "global warming," as the latter phrase sounded less alarming. They tried to stave off calls for urgent action. A lot has changed since then, as the power of words shapes the way people think about climate risks. Government and business leaders gather in Glasgow, and the New York Times climate team has compiled a list of terms you are likely to hear, along with context and caveats, such as carbon pricing, carbon tax, renewable versus clean energy, and natural gas versus gas. This guide to the climate debate is one where science is clear, yet the language is anything but. 

Net zero is a promise that a country or company makes to ensure they do not make any additional greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. In recent years, a growing number of countries and businesses have made pledges for net zero by various dates. The United States and China have made net zero promises, as have Amazon and Apple. In theory, net zero sounds like a good idea, but in practice, the concept can be easily abused. Governments and companies pledge net zero while often promising to stop carbon dioxide altogether, usually by saying they will reduce fossil fuel emissions from factories, homes, and cars, much of which is offset by whatever they get rid of, such as planting trees or using technology to pull carbon dioxide from the air. This is contentious, as trees absorb carbon but can also burn in wildfires. Carbon removal technology still faces criticism, as leaders and businesses use uncertain promises to avoid making deeper cuts today. 

Many net zero pledges are vague and yet are not backed by concrete policies to curb emissions. It is true that in the United States and China, many corporate net zero pledges have been made, with companies pledging for clean offices, for instance, and broader supply chains. It is possible to set rigorous net zero targets, but promises usually need plenty of scrutiny. Brad says that sustainability is getting harder to believe, as claims of sustainability are ubiquitous. A quick online search offers a vast selection of products branded as sustainable, including gift boxes, complete wooden shirts, and toilet paper that encourages users to use less—one sheet at a time. In many cases, it is even unclear which company is claiming sustainability without independent verification. The term can backfire in the case of cotton bags, as serious sustainability means reducing consumption, not just consumer goods. 

In the industry, airlines, restaurants, and banking, fossil fuel companies are often named when discussing companies marketing sustainability, which often has little backing. The United Nations states that sustainability needs to be present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs. True sustainability means bringing humans into balance with the planet's resources, which requires transformative changes and hard work. We get nothing less than saving the world. The carbon footprint is a useful concept that the industry uses to say they decide on a nice dinner, knowing that gas in the atmosphere helps make cattle a sizable source of greenhouse gas emissions. Glasses of California wine and the water on the table generate emissions produced while traveling to the table, and the amount adds to the tally of emissions related to everything else in life, including heating homes, driving to work, and even pet food for cats and dogs. 

The carbon footprint contributes to global warming, and researchers have developed the idea of the carbon footprint as a legitimate sustainability research tool. It was invented by an oil giant, but critics say the fossil fuel industry opted for the idea to focus attention on individual actions and responsibility rather than the wider structural changes needed to rein in emissions, including a much faster shift toward clean renewable energy. The carbon footprint is still a useful concept, though, as it allows us to see that the carbon footprint of a typical American is many times that of a resident of the global south. Yes, individual actions matter; for example, frequent flying has a huge carbon footprint. 

The term "climate disaster" is used by climate scientists and disaster experts to refer to completely different scenarios. In the context of climate change, it refers to anything that reduces emissions of planet-warming gases. We think of the shift from coal-fired electricity generation to wind and solar, and from gas-powered cars to electric vehicles, as energy-efficient without significant progress. Quickly, the planet faces catastrophe, which means something else entirely among emergency managers and disaster experts who use the term to talk about protecting people from the effects of storms and wildfires. Climate experts sometimes refer to this as adaptation. Adaptation, as a counterpart, refers to steps aimed at addressing the current consequences of climate change and preparing for what happens as it gets worse. Good examples include changing how we build houses and roads, helping people move away from places vulnerable to flooding and wildfires, and planting different kinds of trees as weather patterns change. 

The term "resilience" is important, as there are differences. Resilience means maintaining a way of life with better protection, while adaptation means changing the way of life, which is becoming hard to sustain. Think of protecting a beach town from hurricanes as resilience versus helping people move somewhere else as adaptation. Adaptation has been used as a dirty word among environmentalists, viewed as an admission of failure to cut emissions and an invitation to try to cope with the effects of climate change as it gets worse. Criticism has faded, as we need to adapt while still trying to cut emissions. The term still carries weight, especially for poorer communities and nations that have far less ability to adapt. Groups like Christopher's advocate for nature-based solutions to help solve human problems, often climate-related ones. 

For example, meadows and forests act as carbon sinks, keeping greenhouse gases out of the air, while cities and towns with trees cool people during heat waves and protect against storms. Nature-based solutions help fight climate change and guard against its consequences. They are also a critical tool for companies looking for ways to achieve net zero emissions without substantive cuts in fossil fuel use. Science is clear: nature can store enough greenhouse gases to keep the atmosphere anywhere near current rates. Moreover, nature-based solutions are threatened by climate change, as forests burn in intense wildfires and waters rise, releasing greenhouse gases unless nature-based solutions are combined with drastic reductions in fossil fuel emissions. 

Carbon capture, along with its cousin carbon removal, is a way to keep carbon out of the atmosphere. In the first place, since burning fossil fuels remains widespread, engineers are exploring strategies to capture and remove the resulting carbon dioxide. In fact, there are two broad ideas, though there are plenty of question marks. Carbon capture generally refers to technology that traps carbon dioxide coming from factories or power plants before it escapes into the atmosphere and warms the planet. The captured carbon dioxide can either be buried underground permanently or turned into a useful product like concrete. Carbon removal, on the other hand, generally refers to pulling carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, which can be naturally done through trees. Naturally, planting forests is a form of carbon removal, although much land is required for this. Companies are also exploring technological carbon removal, like direct air capture, which are basically giant fans that pull carbon from the sky and inject it underground. 

Carbon removal technology is even less developed than carbon capture, and it is usually far more expensive, though scientists say it is necessary if we want to reach net zero emissions and draw carbon from the atmosphere in order to reverse the global warming already caused. Brad also refers to this as climate intervention, depending on carbon removal, which is sometimes called deliberately intervening in the composition of the atmosphere. This term is also used to describe something entirely different: carbon removal that reflects energy back into space, sometimes called solar geoengineering. Scientists say this could quickly and temporarily reduce global temperatures, but the sort of measure the world needs to cut emissions is wildly controversial. Even if such a scheme worked, nobody is sure of the effects in different parts of the world, as regions could see devastating reductions in rainfall and changes in weather patterns. 

Even conducting basic research into solar geoengineering is viewed by many as morally creating risks for society. The debate continues about whether to block or intensify the effects of climate change, as the world starts to run out of time. Better options are necessary. Christopher discusses the electric car future, which sells an array of vehicles that can be confusing. What does it mean for your chances of actually driving one? It means emissions start to decrease, and sometimes this is just called a chance. Knowing someone drives a hybrid or electric vehicle, even one from Toyota, is significant. The first gas-electric hybrid technology in the auto industry used an electric motor to assist the gasoline engine, greatly cutting the amount of gas the car needed. A plug-in hybrid vehicle is simply an extension of this technology, generally running just on battery power when charging at a station, while the gasoline engine kicks in for regular hybrid vehicles, which are charged via the energy generated when the car slows down. 

Multiple studies have found that battery electric vehicles generally have lower emissions, depending on the local power grid and the environmental impacts to consider. Fuel cell vehicles, powered rather than by batteries, also produce emissions in the form of water vapor, as they are currently produced mainly from natural gas, a fossil fuel. Everywhere requires significant new investments in infrastructure, alongside growing charging infrastructure, which raises questions about climate clean energy. People often confuse renewable energy with clean energy, as people generally use the term to refer to sources of energy that add significant greenhouse gases to the atmosphere, usually contrasting them with fossil fuels like coal, gas, and oil. Renewable energy sources like wind and solar power are broadly considered clean, although the manufacturing of wind and solar panels adds a relatively small amount of carbon to the air. 

Nuclear power plants are often considered clean since they release no carbon dioxide while generating electricity, but everyone agrees that the waste left by nuclear plants is not considered renewable, as the fuel supplies are large. Industry groups sometimes refer to natural gas as clean since it produces less carbon dioxide and far fewer air pollutants than coal when burned. However, natural gas still produces a significant amount of carbon. Wind, solar, and nuclear power use lead to leaks of this potent greenhouse gas. 

The question of natural gas is a natural one, as environmental groups have started to ask whether gas powers homes, which is also a fossil fuel. Fossil fuels are the main drivers of human-caused climate change. Technically, natural gas occurs naturally in the ground alongside oil. In the United States, companies often extract gas using water, sand, and chemicals under high pressure to fracture rock, a process that is hardly natural. Critics say they have started to call it natural gas to make a point. The debate swirling around gas is that while gas burns cleaner than coal, the oil industry has long referred to it as renewable energy. Scientific research has started to show that drilling for gas releases large amounts of potent greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, and emissions play a big role in warming the planet, especially in the shorter term. 

Scientists now say that the world is investing in new pipelines and gas infrastructure, and nations are using gas for decades to come. A growing chorus of critics suggests that yet another name for natural gas is simply gas. Anything that is said in financial terms is often heard as an acronym in relation to retirement mutual funds, investing in profitable companies, and trying to adopt better practices that make a negative impact. This has become increasingly popular in American investments, as companies are now labeled with letters that stand for environmental, social, and governance criteria. This grew to 17 trillion dollars today, with a third of investment assets in the United States falling under the broad category of sustainable responsible investing. 

The kind of company designation is much like the term sustainability, but there is little agreement on what it actually means. There is also considerable debate about whether a company can abide by the three principles. For instance, an equipment company that puts workers first while supplying the fossil fuel industry or a renewable energy company with poor labor practices could both be entitled to carry the label. Carbon emissions at the end of life and the effects of products are classified by agencies that issue ratings that align with general public views on social responsibility. Last year, a major tobacco company was recognized as a leading company among recognizable consumer products brands, including a number named among the top plastic investing. Impact investing focuses on companies whose primary goal is to impact society positively. 

General investing is one of the forces keeping pressure on companies to prioritize environmental and social commitments. Critics say it is time for government regulators to require companies to report the underlying data that makes their claims credible, including diversity data and carbon emissions numbers. Outside regulators, Winston discusses carbon pricing, which market-based economists have long argued is an elegant way to tackle climate change by charging companies and consumers for the emissions they produce. This gives people ample incentive to burn less oil, coal, and gas and shift to cleaner energy practices. Of course, this is complicated, as there are two main ways to implement carbon pricing: a carbon tax, which is usually just a flat tax on oil, gas, and coal in countries like Canada and Sweden, or a cap-and-trade system where the government sets a cap on overall emissions and steadily lowers the cap over time. 

Large permits are issued for every ton of carbon dioxide, and the number of permits decreases over time, driving up the price. California and the European Union have cap-and-trade systems, although designing these programs is tricky. Carbon pricing is a way to implement climate policy, and many governments, including states like California, prefer to directly regulate fuel efficiency in cars and trucks or mandate electric vehicles rather than using carbon prices to make gasoline expensive so consumers opt for cleaner vehicles. In the United States, states have opted to mandate renewable energy directly rather than using carbon pricing for clean power plants.

Disease declared eliminated for years, but cases of measles outbreak raise questions and answers about everything you want to know. The live weakened form of the measles virus inside the vaccine is a virus grown in a culture of salt and human blood, which is called along with what gets added to help stabilize it. The lab-built version of the natural measles virus acts the way a person gets the injection. Children vaccinated receive two doses of the vaccine: the first at months old and the second at years old. Infants months old traveling to the United States or another country should receive one dose of the vaccine beforehand. Adults can get vaccinated; it is never too late. In fact, with measles occurring in the community, it is a good idea to get vaccinated unless you are sure you previously received two shots of the vaccine. The three diseases the vaccine protects against give lifelong immunity, and a booster dose is never needed. Born after the vaccine was made available a decade ago, virtually every child got measles by age. The CDC considers people born before likely to have had measles. Children who received the vaccine should consider getting immunized, as one or two vaccines available may be ineffective. The CDC says the effective vaccine lasts for years, while the ineffective one may not. If you are unsure, consult a doctor. Getting measles twice is nearly impossible, as children develop immunity simply by contracting and recovering from the disease. For people getting vaccinated, you might be thinking that the concept of herd immunity means a large number of people are protected from the disease by the vaccine, making the disease less likely and diminishing the risk for people who are unvaccinated. The threshold for herd immunity varies by disease; for highly contagious diseases, a high percentage of people need to be vaccinated to meet the threshold.

Linking a rare disorder to the Johnson & Johnson COVID vaccine, the real risk appears small. The syndrome associated with the Johnson & Johnson vaccine is known, and federal officials said Monday that the beleaguered COVID vaccine is linked to a small increased risk of this rare, potentially serious condition. The Food and Drug Administration added a warning about this potential side effect, noting that the vaccine's risk appears small so far, based on reports of the syndrome in people who received the Johnson & Johnson vaccine. Nearly a million doses of the vaccine have been administered in the United States. 

Here are answers to common questions about the syndrome in connection with vaccination. The syndrome is a rare condition in which the immune system attacks nerve cells, often beginning in the hands and feet and progressing to widespread muscle weakness and even paralysis. In mild cases, symptoms pass within weeks, while serious cases can result in hospitalization and, in rare instances, death. The condition can also cause permanent nerve damage. In the United States, there are typically 1,500 cases of the syndrome per year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and it is common among adults.

The Trump administration escalates the global fight over tech in Washington. The Trump administration said Tuesday it would open an investigation into the taxes on digital commerce adopted by the proposed nine countries and the European Union, escalating the global battle that affects big American tech companies like Facebook and Amazon. These taxes could ultimately lead to American tariffs on imports from Brazil, Britain, and India, which are host countries with chances of another global trade dispute resulting in retaliatory taxes on goods. The investigation is conducted by the United States Trade Representative and could also complicate global negotiations underway this year aimed at reaching a multinational consensus on taxing internet commerce. List frequently asked questions about the King Supreme Court case implications for Obamacare. The Obamacare case is back in the Supreme Court, frequently asked questions about the King case are important. Back at the top, the case has been one of the years' important news subjects, with the potential roll back of a major portion of Obamacare subsidies affecting millions of middle-income people across states who now receive help to buy health insurance. Without subsidies, many people are unable to afford health insurance, and without people in the insurance markets, prices have risen for everyone else. The government's victory means the health care law will continue unchanged. The court ruled back at the top decision; the Supreme Court ruled that subsidies will continue to be distributed to insurance customers in every state of the country, regardless of whether they ran a marketplace. Congress passed the Affordable Care Act to improve health insurance markets, not to destroy them, wrote Chief Justice John Roberts in the court's majority opinion in the case back at the top. The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, the health law's official name, sets up every state for people to shop for individual health plans. Blue states set up what are known as exchanges, while red states instead allow the federal government across states. About 87 percent of customers qualify for federal subsidies to help pay for coverage based on income. One section of the law says subsidies flow to customers in exchanges established by states. The plaintiffs argued unsuccessfully that the language meant people in state-run exchanges would federally run exchanges not get subsidies. This means states back at the top using the federal exchange no longer need to worry about losing health insurance subsidies for their residents. Now, states managing health insurance exchanges think twice about whether it is worth the continued expense and difficulty. Already, several state exchanges have switched to the federal platform, and others are considering it. People affected back at the top, beyond the immediate cancellation of subsidies, face a decision. The plaintiffs also have secondary effects on insurance markets; if subsidies disappeared, lower-income customers would drop out of the market, and patients are likely to keep paying for insurance, which in turn could lead to higher prices for everyone, including people who use subsidies.

Fifty years ago, Mao unleashed a decade-long political upheaval intended to transform China. Key events, people, and issues of the Cultural Revolution are explained. Fifty years ago, Mao unleashed the Cultural Revolution, a decade-long upheaval with dramatic, often violent effects across China. The tumultuous years of the Cultural Revolution movement fundamentally altered elite politics, as Mao tried to control the setting with radical youths in the Communist Party, leading to widespread consequences at various levels of society. Young people battled perceived enemies among one another, and Red Guards were sent to the countryside in the later stages of the Cultural Revolution. People deemed to have ties to the West or the former Nationalist government, as well as many officials like future leaders, were eventually killed or committed suicide, leaving a permanent mark. Scholars contend that the trauma of the era contributed to the economic transition in the decades that followed, as the Chinese were willing to embrace market-oriented reforms to spur growth. This ease took place after the Chinese Communist Central Committee issued outlined ideas for the Cultural Revolution. In the months and years leading to the end, considered after Mao's death in September, the subsequent arrest of the Gang of Four, a radical faction of four political leaders including Mao's wife, occurred in October. Although the Cultural Revolution lasted a decade, much of the extreme violence occurred in the first years. The roots of the Cultural Revolution can be traced back to the Great Leap Forward, which left many millions dead, as Mao was partly blamed for sidelining Communist Party leaders and pulling back extreme efforts.

Inflation, as explained in the FAQ card, refers to the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning that a dollar today is worth less than a dollar tomorrow. Inflation is typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, furniture, apparel, and transportation. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, and inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Inflation can be bad, depending on the circumstances; fast price increases spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. 

Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market; rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms. Tangible assets like houses have held their value better. Trump also advocated for reducing the corporate income tax rate from the current percent to a proposed percent. This proposal comes after a decade in which corporate profits have risen sharply while the share of national income going to compensation for workers has fallen.

The results provided the first clinical evidence that the vaccine can prevent COVID disease, including severe cases, the chief executive Albert tweeted. Moderna and other companies announced their findings in news releases, but peer-reviewed scientific disclosure of detailed data will allow outside experts to evaluate the claims; therefore, the results are considered preliminary and figures on effectiveness may change as studies continue. The products open the door to an entirely new way of creating vaccines, using a fast version of the coronavirus genetic material called messenger RNA to program cells to make many copies of the virus, which sets off alarms in the immune system to attack the real virus if it tries to invade. Although a number of vaccines using this technology are in development, none have yet been approved for marketing. In fact, two different vaccines made by two different companies have two different kinds of structures, but the new messenger RNA concept worked effectively, confirming that the concept is a viable strategy against COVID and future infectious disease threats, said Barry, a professor of public health at Harvard and dean at the University of Florida. He said it is an important finding that the vaccine appeared to prevent severe forms of the disease. Pfizer has released information on disease severity, reporting results from researchers who say that the positive results from the Pfizer and Moderna vaccine candidates tested aim to target a part called the spike protein of the coronavirus, which it uses to invade human cells. The success of the two vaccines means that measures of immunity used in earlier studies, such as antibody levels, are reliable, and companies will use these measures as proof of effectiveness in the testing and approval process for the vaccines.

Inflation is a frequently asked question; inflation means the loss of purchasing power over time, which is typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, and inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in little economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Inflation can be bad, but it depends on the circumstances; fast price increases spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor, and it is especially hard on the shoulders of poor households that spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market; rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better. Ransomware virus computer criminals demand money to unlock and become a lucrative online scheme, with ransomware expanding in the United States. People fall testament to increasingly targeted methods. Early variations of ransomware locked computers and displayed images, while Russian criminals demanded a fee that was often removed. Current variants target researchers, and criminals now use internet addresses and notes instead of images. Criminals flash messages to local law enforcement agencies, accusing victims of visiting illegal gambling sites and demanding they pay a fine to unlock their computer. Victims in the United States see messages in English from the FBI and the Justice Department, while people in the Netherlands receive similar messages from Dutch local police. Irish variations even demand money. The latest variants speak to victims through recorded audio messages, telling users to pay within hours or face criminal charges, and even show footage of law enforcement watching. These messages often demand that victims buy a card purchased locally and enter a PIN, making it impossible for victims to cancel the transaction. It becomes clear that the criminals' intention is to hunt down and find gangs. Researchers have identified ransomware gangs and tracked one gang that tried to infect a computer in a single day. Even researchers tracking internet addresses find catching those responsible difficult, as it requires cooperation among global law enforcement. Criminals are skilled at destroying evidence. Charlie, an independent security researcher based in France, was able to hack one of the computers and discover just one victim from one day last month. Accounting showed that they were able to infect computers in 10 percent of attempts, with 5 percent paying in cases where hackers demanded 1,000 euros, making a haul of 1 million euros from one work.

Studies find that people with COVID who receive a single dose of the Pfizer vaccine have enough to provide robust protection against the coronavirus, according to two new studies from Britain published late Thursday in a prominent medical journal. These studies are among the first fully published papers to weigh the benefits of vaccinating people with COVID and add strong evidence to the case that people already have antibodies to the virus after one dose of the Pfizer vaccine. One study, led by researchers from University College London and Public Health England, described the benefits of this strategy as potentially accelerating vaccine rollout, which could help turn the tide against dangerous new mutations in coverage without compromising vaccine-induced immunity and help reduce variant emergence, the paper said.
