Inflation FAQ card: Inflation is the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning a dollar today is worth less than a dollar tomorrow. It is typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. Causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand. Inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. 

Inflation can be bad, but it depends on the circumstances. Fast price increases spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation can also affect the stock market; rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general. Historically, tangible assets like houses have held their value better than financial markets during inflation booms.

State representative threatened to introduce legislation to bar local governments from implementing business companies' policies, business news reported in March. Giant credit reporting companies keep files on roughly 200 million Americans, and they said on Friday they will soon wipe away credit created by certain medical debts. Changes include removing black marks for people who settled debts that went to collections, which cheered consumer advocates and reflected a growing acceptance that debts do not represent the best financial behavior. Companies said the changes will eliminate 70 percent of medical debt accounts from credit reports, which contain data used to calculate the important three-digit credit score key for mortgages, car loans, and rental agreements. Starting in July, medical debts paid that went to collections will no longer appear on credit reports, which currently linger for seven years. New unpaid medical debts will now appear for a full year after being sent to collections instead of the current six months, giving people time to address the debt with insurance companies and health care providers. Beginning in the first half of 2024, credit reporting companies said they will exclude unpaid medical collection debts. The industry remains committed to helping drive fair and affordable access to credit for consumers, the chief executives said in a statement. The changes mirror actions already taken elsewhere that are used to generate credit scores, which have already been updated to reduce the influence of paid medical debts. Older scoring models still widely used do not necessarily benefit consumers. Three changes, for example, include unpaid medical debts reducing negative information flowing into calculations. Lenders have adopted the latest updates, and there is huge doubt, said a staff attorney at the National Consumer Law Center, which helps people with medical debt due to things like high bills that usually change little. This lift in scores for people with the largest unpaid debts often results from catastrophic and costly illnesses, even with insurance coverage. The poorest and most vulnerable 20 percent added, referring to the portion of unpaid medical debt accounts that remain on credit reports. The widely used credit score changes ignore paid debts and weigh certain unpaid medical collections less heavily. Starting with a formula found to ignore collection accounts for medical debts that were otherwise paid actually improves accuracy. It has been eliminated entirely, and it was also found that people with unpaid medical collections are less risky than types of unpaid collections. Information on people with unpaid accounts, including medical, still remains. However, none of this is far from eliminating medical debt altogether. A main competitor made similar changes to its formula even earlier, eliminating paid collections, including medical debt, from its scoring model. A vice president of scores analytics said the company is working with credit reporting companies on these changes to shift scores for many people affected. It is believed that these changes will have a similar effect, as reporting companies eliminated two sources of negative information, such as tax liens and civil judgments. Affected consumers generally saw their scores rise by 20 points or less, said a consumer. Otherwise, if a credit report eliminated a medical bill that was paid, it could boost a score by 50 points. Added scores in the range of 700 are better, as a file that looks good takes away negative information, leading to a score increase. The announcements came just weeks after the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau said it would scrutinize the credit treatment of medical debt and consider an outright ban on including medical debt in credit reports. The agency said research suggested roughly 43 million people have medical bills on their credit reports, with around $58 billion—fifty-eight percent of collections debt—appearing on credit reports tied to medical bills. The bureau estimated that medical debts are often difficult to resolve given the insurance system's practices, and sometimes consumers are not even aware of unpaid bills on credit reports, which can apply to loan scores and lead to lower expectations. Federal law prohibits employers from discriminating against people with disabilities and requires them to make reasonable accommodations. Research has found that discrimination remains common; one study found that job applications that disclosed a disability were 40 percent less likely to receive interest from prospective employers. Even finding jobs, workers with disabilities frequently encounter barriers to success, such as bathroom doors that open without assistance. Hostile workers and groups of workers with disabilities face obstacles to employment, as criminal records tend to benefit disproportionately from strong job markets, giving employers an incentive to seek talent quickly. Opportunities can quickly dry up, and in the last recession, the labor market for disabled people was often among the last to recover. "First in, last out," said Adam, chief economist at the Economic Innovation Group, a Washington research organization. Remote work, however, has the potential to break this cycle, as at least one new study found that employment has risen for workers with disabilities across industries as the labor market improved. Many economists believe that the shift toward remote work, unlike the red-hot labor market, is likely to prove lasting. The purpose is to ensure that the federal government is providing reliable information upon which policies affect the citizens of the state of Oklahoma. Based on the EPA's issued background technical support document titled 'Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reporting from the Petroleum and Natural Gas Industry,' the report indicates that the EPA altered the methodology previously used to estimate emissions from natural gas production. The EPA estimated tons per completion for conventional natural gas wells, while the new estimates hold that gas wells produce tons per completion. As a result, the new estimates show that the EPA adjusted prior year reports far back to reflect these new estimates, which read significant increases. We began to question the methodology used to create these estimates, as the significant increases in estimates raise questions about the methodology used to create them. A recent report exploring the methodology for determining emissions from natural gas production convinced us that these questions are valid. A highly respected research firm with specific expertise in the oil and natural gas production sector released a report entitled 'Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Natural Gas Development.' This report points out specific flaws that the EPA made in its analysis, including the inaccurate application of natural gas STAR program data collected from a small number of wells, which assumes industry rates based on flawed data points from the nearest hundred thousand or even ten thousand, thus overcoming the high uncertainty in the industry. The best operators in Oklahoma assume that producers capture their product, which is flat wrong. The flaws listed, among many others, led the EPA to apply inaccurate statistics in research reports. Certainly, this study included several inaccurate assumptions that make the basis of its review lies in the emissions developed by the EPA. The Cornell study's estimates find a voice in government studies, and the Department of Energy's natural gas subcommittee report even mentions the conclusion that the greenhouse gas footprint of gas production and use is founded on inaccurate data, casting doubt upon the entire industry. The EPA, in announcing new proposals to regulate emissions from production facilities, used significantly flawed estimates that show economic harm to domestic producers. In fact, even the EPA uses incorrect assumptions to claim that the rule will quickly result in net savings of nearly million annually for domestic producers. We assure you that estimates must be properly developed to provide the citizens of the state of Oklahoma with the proper tools to determine the accuracy of the EPA's data, reports, and studies that justify current and future EPA regulatory proposals. We ask that you provide our office with the following information: information regarding the determination of natural gas estimates, information related to appropriate rounding rates to the nearest hundred thousand or ten thousand per completion, which produce inaccurate end estimates, and information explaining how the EPA improperly assumed natural gas STAR data records for natural gas collected green, including the conclusion that the process is appropriate for determining wells. We also request information explaining how the EPA concluded that Oklahoma natural gas producers commonly capture emissions and reduce them, simply because Oklahoma regulators mandate this. Lastly, we ask for information explaining how the EPA estimates are accurate for natural gas producers who allow significant product to escape into the atmosphere rather than being captured and marketed. Existing and proposed potential rules and regulations are based on the EPA's estimates for natural gas wells. According to the Chinese proposal, the leader would be chosen by popular vote, starting with candidates who first win the endorsement of at least half of the members of the nominating committee. The composition of the committee would be based on the current election committee, according to a decision announced at the Great Hall of the People. It said the existing committee already denies the Hong Kong electorate the right to form the basis of the nominating committee for future elections. This assertion was rejected by Hong Kong democrats, and democracy advocates expect the new committee to be like the existing one, which excludes candidates seen as unfavorable to Beijing. "The composition will ensure that democrats have no chance of getting nominated," said Michael Davis, a law professor at the University of Hong Kong. In fact, he said it raises the bar for candidates to win one-eighth support, while the current committee requires them to win 50 percent. The new guidelines, as far as we can see, limit the government's capacity to offer a deal to democrats. The Chinese government fears that direct nominations would allow candidates hostile to Beijing, and said direct nominations also contradict the Basic Law, the document governing Hong Kong's relationship with the mainland. The Daily Main newspaper, affiliated with the Chinese Communist Party, said in an editorial on Monday that the central government has never allowed anyone to become chief executive without its approval. A storm front moved into Hong Kong on Sunday as protesters began gathering at the legislature after the announcement of the decision. The territory's credit is at stake, according to Alex, an agent for France Presse and Getty Images. The Hong Kong government plans to use the Chinese proposal as a framework for the electoral reform bill, which must win approval from members of the Legislative Council, but democratic members are still blocking its passage, which requires a two-thirds majority. Emily, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Democratic Party, said she would veto the proposal on Sunday.

NYC Pass is the New York vaccine passport app, launching on March first as a government-issued vaccine passport app for the country. Applications from the city and state vaccination records have provided a million New Yorkers with a printed pass since its debut, according to the State Department of Health. To get the pass, users can download it from Apple and Android app stores. The app finds the official record for people vaccinated in New York State and issues a pass containing a unique code certifying that they are vaccinated. This code is generated days after a person is fully vaccinated and can be stored on their phone or printed. To find a vaccination record, the app checks the name, date of birth, and code against the county vaccination records. Nearly all information must match the vaccination agency entered. The Federal Reserve, like many central banks, sets policy with an eye on the domestic economy to battle control of prices, causing pain abroad and global fallout. Rate moves to stop the Fed from raising higher rates slow inflation, cooling consumer demand and allowing supply to catch up, which moderates price increases. This process slows hiring, weakens wage growth, and prompts job losses that ripple through financial markets in sometimes disruptive ways. Much pain from these moves ultimately causes remains unclear, as many countries are raising rates quickly, making it difficult to determine when an intense slowdown takes full effect. Monetary policy takes months or years to kick in completely, and many economists and several international bodies have warned of pronounced danger, including a United Nations agency that warned the damage is particularly acute for poorer nations and developing economies already dealing with a cost of living crisis and soaring food and fuel prices. Now, American imports are growing steadily more expensive as the dollar marches higher, with moves spurred by market volatility and worries about financial stability. Higher rates elevate the value of the dollar, making it harder for emerging market borrowers to pay back dollar debt, which is a recipe for global turmoil, even recession. Despite this, the Fed is poised to continue raising interest rates, as the Fed, like central banks around the world, charges towards domestic economy goals that are supposed to keep inflation slow and steady while achieving maximum employment, occasionally called the banker position. The Fed goes about its day-to-day business with its eye squarely on America.

Move effectively creates a new federal agency, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the Food and Drug Administration. The Biden administration's division will broadly oversee pandemic responses, as shown in an image of Dawn, the Assistant Secretary for Response at the Department of Health and Human Services, credited to Greg Agence France Presse via Pool via Getty Images. The Biden administration is creating a new division within the Department of Health and Human Services to coordinate the response to pandemic threats and health emergencies, recognizing that the department is equipped to handle disasters like the coronavirus pandemic. The change, announced internally on Wednesday, will elevate the existing Office of the Assistant Secretary for Response, known as the Operating Division for Administration Strategic Response. This move effectively creates a new federal agency, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the Food and Drug Administration, responsible for crucial health logistics, including oversight of the Strategic National Stockpile, emergency medical reserve contracting, and distributing vaccines in emergencies. The aim is to increase authority and consolidate powers to operate alongside counterparts like the CDC and FDA, as well as the National Institutes of Health, to manage various aspects of emergency response. It may also create tensions between agencies and campuses outside Washington. The new division will operate from headquarters in the capital. The change allows for a mobilized, coordinated national response quickly to future disasters and emergencies, with greater hiring and contracting capabilities. Dawn, the Assistant Secretary for Response, wrote to employees in a Wednesday email announcing the change, which was first reported by the Washington Post. The surface office of the division seems like a Washington bureaucratic entity, but people familiar with the change say the new division will build on the work of the response office, which already has capabilities built during the pandemic. It will be in charge of the National Stockpile, which was previously run by the CDC, and was bitterly opposed by the stockpile for being short on basic supplies, including ventilators, masks, and protective gear at the outset of the pandemic. It stands today as a searing example of failures in the early response. The new division also already oversees the Advanced Research and Development Authority, which is responsible for developing innovative vaccines, thrusting the agency into the spotlight. President Donald Trump fired the director at the start of the pandemic, and the Assistant Secretary running it lacked the capability to contract companies to purchase vaccines, forcing them to rely on the Department of Defense to handle the purchasing and distribution of shots. The Office of the Operating Division will enable them to take on these responsibilities, according to people familiar with the move. The memo said that new hiring and contracting authority would be in place, but overseeing the National Stockpile limits typical staff decisions, which appeared to catch top federal health officials by surprise, including the White House and CDC senior officials. Lawrence, a former CDC adviser who directs the Institute for National and Global Health Law at Georgetown University, said the announcement on Wednesday was a little vague and makes it seem like one agency is badly needed for key functions of another agency. "Even if they think it will happen, the consequence is the right answer to fix," he said, raising concerns about the agency going back to the days before the Biden administration and future administrations. A spokeswoman for the CDC said the agency is supportive of the Assistant Secretary's vision and is a critical partner in addressing public health, continuing to work closely together to advance and protect the health of the American people. A spokeswoman for a former acting chief scientist at the FDA and a National Security Council official said the office was always meant to be a strategic arm of the federal health bureaucracy, but operationally, one must be careful that the new entity becomes operational with clear responsibilities. They said there is a need to leverage the whole government, as changes in authority and responsibility could create confusion, with the CDC playing an essential role in the response.

Pfizer-BioNTech said on Wednesday that they are now applying to the Food and Drug Administration for approval of the coronavirus vaccine booster shot for those aged 16 and older. They will submit supporting data by the end of the week. This move came after the companies said that the third shot of the vaccine sharply increased levels of antibodies against the virus. The companies conducted a study with volunteers who received the booster shot five to eight months after the second shot. Researchers found that the level of antibodies that block the coronavirus jumped to three times higher than the level after the second dose, with side effects from the third injection similar to those of the initial two doses. The companies said that the underlying data is included in the news release, along with the dates and location of the study. They also said they are preparing a scientific publication describing the research. The news of Pfizer's booster application came two days after the FDA fully approved the two-dose vaccine for older adults, making it the first move beyond emergency use status.

Public health authorities in Denmark and Norway on Monday released grim projections of the coming wave of the omicron coronavirus variant, predicting it will dominate in these countries in a matter of days. Although scientists do not yet know how often the variant causes severe disease, they say the rapid rate of spread could lead to an explosion of cases, potentially increasing pressure on hospitals. Even if it proves mild, reports follow similarly worrisome findings from England released over the weekend, although researchers caution that the trend may change as the variant comes into clearer view. It is not yet certain how often omicron infections send people to the hospital, and many hospitalized patients are likely to die from omicron, which partly evades immune defenses. Researchers have yet to determine how well vaccinations and previous infections protect people from severe disease. Authors of new reports also observed that swift actions, such as booster campaigns, are reducing opportunities for omicron to spread. American researchers have yet to release models predicting the rise in the United States, but experts point to the country having similar vaccination levels to Norway and Denmark, as well as certain COVID risk factors like the average age of the population.

The reason Democrats failed to retake the House is probably due to the reason that next year the debate on gerrymandering will be crucial to hold the House. Similarly, the Democratic margin of victory in the House and the popular vote is simply too large by a single percentage point. Political scientists needed to find alternative explanations for the Republican edge, as the tendency of Democrats to receive votes heavily from Democratic cities accounts for the percentage point saw. Gerrymandering is assumed to be the main cause of the GOP victory, but alternative explanations added virtually nothing to the Republican edge. There is little question that geography helps bias the House playing field against Democrats. Perhaps the best established effect in American elections is that Republicans entered the election with many seats, while Democrats faced a geographic disadvantage that made it harder to clearly establish. There is little doubt that Democrats routinely win over 60 percent of the vote in big cities, which are worth many congressional districts, while places where Republicans win over 50 percent of the vote have enough people to form a congressional district. As a result, the remaining vote in the remaining districts favors Republicans. Minnesota emerged as a compelling example, as the map was drawn by a judicial panel appointed by the state supreme court, and the Democratic governor rejected plans from the Republican-led legislature. Hillary Clinton won the state but took three out of eight congressional districts, while Donald Trump won the median congressional district by eight points. This means that Democrats win in districts favored by Trump, and the clear margin to claim a majority of congressional districts makes Minnesota a compelling case in political geography. Presidential elections have shifted to become like the rest of the country, and it is rare for Democrats to be competitive even among rural voters. The typical pattern shows big Democratic strength in cities and Republican strength in the countryside, which has become a typical Democratic disadvantage. It is hard to measure the effect of political geography on the Democratic disadvantage nationwide, but it is much harder to argue that gerrymandering is the clear cause of the real effects. It is hard to argue that geography made a difference in the failure to take the House.

The number of Americans quitting jobs is at the highest record, as workers take advantage of strong employer demand to pursue better opportunities. In November, a million people voluntarily left jobs, the Labor Department said Tuesday, while two million left in October. For two decades, the government has been keeping track of the surge in quitting in recent months, along with the continuing difficulty reported by employers in filling positions. This underscores a strange and contradictory moment facing the economy two years into pandemic-induced disruptions. There has been much discussion about the increase in quitting, sometimes referred to as the Great Resignation, which has focused on white-collar workers evaluating their priorities. Job turnover has concentrated in hospitality and low-wage sectors, where there is intense competition for employees. Given this, workers have leverage to seek better pay. The Great Resignation story is really about lower-wage workers finding new opportunities as the reopening labor market allows them to seize better conditions, said Nick, director of economic research at Indeed. The hiring lab indicates that the rush to reopen the economy has created a rare opportunity for workers to demand better pay and working conditions, allowing them to change jobs easily in sectors where demand is strong. Pay gains have been modest, overwhelmed by faster inflation. Data from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta shows that jobs are getting significantly faster pay increases for people who stay in their jobs. Faster pay increases and faster inflation are at least partly the result of the remarkable strength of the economic recovery. After collapsing in the first weeks of the pandemic, consumer spending quickly rebounded and eventually reached record levels, helped by hundreds of billions of dollars in federal aid. Businesses suddenly struggled to keep up with demand, leading to supply chain issues, labor shortages, and rising prices. The stubborn nature of the pandemic contributed to problems in spending patterns, keeping many workers on the sidelines. The number of jobs per month shows signs that the worst turbulence is beginning to ease. Late last year, the number of job postings by employers fell, the Labor Department said Tuesday, though it remained high by historical standards. Hiring picked up, as earlier data showed that people returned to the labor force in November. Various measures indicate that supply chain pressures have begun to ease. The explosion of coronavirus cases linked to the Omicron variant forced airlines to cancel flights and businesses to delay return-to-office plans, while school districts temporarily returned to remote learning. Forecasters say the latest COVID wave brings certain economic uncertainty, though it is unclear how soon it will affect inflation, spending, and the job market despite the demand for workers. This is an increase from 54 percent who were asked the same question a year earlier. The FAQ card on inflation explains that inflation results in the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning that a dollar today is worth less than a dollar tomorrow. Inflation is typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, furniture, apparel, and transportation. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, and inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Whether inflation is bad depends on the circumstances; fast price increases can spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor, and it hits especially hard on the shoulders of poor households that spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market, as rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms. Tangible assets like houses have held their value better. The vaccine developed by the University of Oxford and AstraZeneca has the potential to slow the transmission of the virus, according to a new paper. The paper from researchers at the University of Oxford presents the latest report of evidence suggesting the coronavirus vaccine is able to reduce the transmission of the virus, though scientists emphasized the data is preliminary and the degree of protection is unknown. Researchers measured the impact on transmission among participants every week, seeking to detect signs of the virus; the virus was present even when someone infected did not spread it. They found a percent reduction in positive cases among vaccinated individuals. The paper, which is peer-reviewed, looked at data from clinical trials in Britain, Brazil, and South Africa, with results first reported late last year. Matt, the British health secretary, hailed the results on Wednesday, stating, "Now we know the Oxford vaccine also reduces transmission, which will help get us out of the pandemic," said in an interview on Wednesday morning with BBC. The results, he said, give everyone confidence that it works to keep us safe and to prevent passing the virus. Scientists, looking at the limited information released, cautioned that analysis of the data is needed before broad conclusions can be firmly stated. This is extremely welcome news, but we need the data confirmed. It is important to still continue to follow social distancing guidance even if vaccinated, said Doug Brown, chief executive of the British Society. Oxford AstraZeneca researchers also found that a single dose of the vaccine is percent effective in preventing COVID, with data measured three months after the first shot was given, including the initial three-week period needed for protection to take effect. The encouraging results lend support to the strategy deployed in Britain and other countries to prioritize providing as many first doses of vaccines as possible, setting aside concerns about people getting their second doses later than initially planned. The latest data bears on the debate about whether to space doses of the two vaccines authorized in the United States, Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, since data from candidate vaccines has led scientists to call for the United States to follow the lead of Britain and other countries that opted to delay second doses of vaccines for weeks. Federal officials resisted, saying the move is not supported by data from clinical trials of the two vaccines currently available across the nation. The results amplify pressure on health officials to delay second doses of the vaccine, though it is not yet authorized in the country. The vaccine appeared effective with two shots, longer than originally intended with a four-week gap. Oxford AstraZeneca researchers found that among clinical trial participants who got two standard strength doses at least three months apart, the vaccine is percent effective compared to percent effective for doses given less than six weeks apart. The vaccination strategy of spacing doses three months apart during the rollout of the pandemic is due to limited vaccine supplies in the short term. Researchers wrote that the newly released paper builds on data issued late last year, which found the vaccine to be percent effective when given in two standard strength doses. Initial findings showed efficacy to be much higher at percent for the first dose of the vaccine given at half strength. Oxford AstraZeneca researchers initially attributed the different levels of effectiveness to the lower strength of the initial dose but gradually reached a different conclusion: the amount of time between doses is likely the explanation. The United States Food and Drug Administration is waiting for data from a clinical trial that enrolled participants mostly from America, with results from the study expected later this month. The study is expected to arm AstraZeneca with enough safety data to allow it to seek authorization to provide the vaccine for emergency use in the United States. Disease declared eliminated for far too long, but cases of measles outbreak raise questions and answers about everything you want to know. The live weakened form of the measles virus inside the vaccine is a virus grown in culture from salt and human fetal blood, which helps stabilize the lab-built version of the natural measles virus. This acts the way a person gets the injection. Children vaccinated receive two doses of the vaccine: the first at months old and the second at years old. Infants months old traveling to the United States or another country should receive one dose of the vaccine beforehand. Adults can get vaccinated; it is never too late. In fact, with measles occurring in the community, it is a good idea to get vaccinated unless you are sure you previously received two shots of the vaccine. The three diseases the vaccine protects against give lifelong immunity, and a booster dose is never needed. Born after the vaccine was made available a decade ago, virtually every child got measles by age. The CDC considers people born before this likely to have had measles. Children and people who received the vaccine should consider getting immunized. One or two vaccines available may be ineffective, but the CDC says the effective vaccine lasts for years, while the ineffective one may not. If you are unsure, consult your doctor. Many children develop immunity simply by contracting and recovering from the disease. People getting vaccinated matters. If you are thinking about vaccinating your child, you are probably considering the concept of herd immunity, which means a large number of people are protected from the disease by the vaccine. As the disease is less likely to spread, this diminishes the risk for unvaccinated people. The threshold for herd immunity varies by disease; for highly contagious diseases, a high percentage of people need to be vaccinated to meet the threshold.

Inflation FAQ card: Inflation is the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning the dollar is worth less than it was. Typically, inflation is expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, and inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Whether inflation is bad depends on the circumstances; fast price increases can spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation can also affect the stock market; rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better.

Scientists at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Friday took aim at the question of whether the delta variant of the coronavirus causes severe disease, finding significant differences in the course of hospitalized illnesses during the delta wave compared to earlier in the pandemic. Larger, detailed studies from a number of countries found that people with delta infections are considerably more likely to be hospitalized in the first place. The trend in the CDC study was unable to address limitations in the data. The CDC study also said that the proportion of older hospitalized patients in intensive care dying has shown signs of increasing during the delta wave, which presents a higher level of challenge than earlier versions of the virus. The question of whether the delta variant also causes serious disease swept around the world. The alpha variant, the earlier version first detected in Britain, appeared linked to a higher risk of death, though scientists also tried to understand whether factors besides the variant were playing a role. Studies from England, Scotland, Canada, and Singapore suggested that the delta variant is associated with severe illness, a finding that scientists said raises the risk of outbreaks in unvaccinated areas and puts a bigger burden on health systems. Unlike the CDC study, other studies drew on sequencing, allowing researchers to distinguish infections with the delta variant and track patients entering the hospital. Without access to sequencing data, CDC researchers could not determine which variants patients were infected with. They also examined patients already admitted to hospitals, making it impossible to determine whether there was a higher risk of hospital care in the first place. The study released on Friday examined roughly COVID hospitalizations, comparing July and August when delta dominated with earlier months of the year, and found a significant change in hospitalized outcomes. The study said that the proportion of hospitalized patients aged 65 or older who died or were admitted to intensive care increased during the delta period, though the differences were significant and work is needed. Hospitals included in the study reported that roughly 80 percent of COVID patients were unvaccinated. Researchers said that their findings matched CDC studies using similar methods, which showed significant differences in outcomes for younger people hospitalized during the delta surge. Outside scientists questioned the study. David, an epidemiologist at the University of Toronto, ran a larger study and found that people infected with the delta variant had roughly twice the risk of hospitalization compared to people infected with variants labeled as a concern. He said that analyses are needed to control for a range of factors that affect the course of COVID illnesses, including the availability of vaccines, testing, and treatments, as the pandemic changes. The CDC was really surprised by the small sample of individuals with detailed clinical information, which they used statistical methods to deal with the data. The study drawing on cases published last month also showed significantly increased risks of intensive care admission and death among those infected with the delta variant, accounting for age, sex, and vaccination status factors. Roughly 80 percent of people with delta infections in the study were unvaccinated, while 10 percent were partially vaccinated and 10 percent fully vaccinated, showing that people are heavily protected against COVID. Similarly, a study from Scotland in June based on COVID cases showed that delta infections were associated with a 50 percent higher risk of hospitalization, though it allowed for a wide degree of uncertainty in the precise figure. Data from England drawn from cases published in August found that people infected with the delta variant were just twice as likely to be hospitalized as people infected with the alpha variant, though researchers in the study were unsure of the precise figure. Roughly three-quarters of patients in the study were unvaccinated, while the rest were partially vaccinated.

Massachusetts Senator running for president announced a regulatory plan aimed at breaking large tech companies whose tech mergers illegally undermine competition. Elizabeth Warren proposes breaking tech giants like Amazon and Facebook among a crowded field of Democrats seeking the presidential nomination. Warren has done so by adding detail to early proposals, including a plan for universal child care and a tax on the wealthiest families. On Friday, breaking up big technological giants with a regulatory plan will also force acquisitions by tech giants, her campaign said, including deals like WhatsApp and Instagram, in addition to the Whole Foods purchase. Companies would be barred from sharing data with third parties, and dual entities like Amazon and its marketplace would be split apart. Sign up for the politics newsletter to join the conversation in the presidential race, as pressure builds on elected officials to place additional oversight on tech companies. For months, particularly after revelations that companies like Facebook violated customer privacy agreements, Warren has also been sending a political warning shot across the Democratic primary field. Decisions on how much to embrace or reject Silicon Valley and wealthy donors have become an important dividing line among candidates in the wide-open nomination race. Democrats like Warren, Senator Bernie Sanders from Vermont, and Senator Amy Klobuchar from Minnesota have expressed a willingness to limit the influence of companies like Facebook, Google, Apple, and Amazon, though Sanders and Klobuchar have yet to present clear policy details.
